overview: The file consists of five Department of State “List of Papers” sheets indexing correspondence and memoranda from roughly 1930–1940 about Japanese diplomatic and telegraphic codes. Early entries concern attempts by E. S. Smith and G. Momose to provide photographs, copies, or information about Japanese Foreign Office code books, together with Japanese reactions to Herbert O. Yardley’s disclosures about American decipherment of Japanese messages during the Washington Conference. Most later entries trace the interdepartmental and legal controversy surrounding Yardley’s The American Black Chamber and a proposed book on Japanese diplomatic secrets, including Japanese press coverage, lecture publicity, the 1933 secrecy legislation, Bobbs-Merrill’s unsuccessful requests to continue publication, Customs restrictions on imported editions, and Pocket Books’ 1940 proposal for a low-priced edition. The underlying correspondence is not reproduced in the supplied pages; these sheets function as a detailed archival finding aid to it.

subfiles.title: List of Papers: Telegraph Codes—Japan
subfiles.about: A five-page archival index summarizes papers concerning Japanese government codes and the controversy over Herbert O. Yardley’s publications.
subfiles.summary: The opening entries record offers by E. S. Smith and G. Momose to supply photographs, copies, or information concerning Japanese Foreign Office code books, as well as a Japanese phonetic code reported by Albert L. Woody. The index then documents Japanese press reaction to Yardley’s account of American decipherment during the Washington Conference and State and War Department discussion of the resulting publicity. Later entries follow publishers, legislators, lawyers, and federal departments as they debated The American Black Chamber, Yardley’s proposed Japanese Diplomatic Secrets, and the effect of the Act of June 10, 1933. The final entries concern Customs restrictions on imported editions and the State Department’s 1940 refusal to endorse a Pocket Books edition.

interest: The index captures an unusual transition from attempted acquisition of foreign code material to official efforts to contain public disclosure of American cryptanalytic activity. Its terse entries reveal tensions among intelligence interests, diplomacy, freedom of publication, copyright enforcement, and the federal secrecy legislation of 1933, while also documenting repercussions in the Japanese press. For historians, it is especially useful as a roadmap to otherwise dispersed State, War, Justice, Treasury, congressional, and publishing-industry correspondence, although gaps in the item numbering and the absence of the indexed papers themselves require cautious use.
